deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is a bracketed prose draft, 'Blatt 12', of Riemann's speculative psychology and metaphysics. A later hand added in the right column 'Ist in Blatt 14 enthalten', meaning the content is incorporated in a later sheet. The tightly cropped numbers 1), 2), 3), 4), 7), 8), 10), 11) on the right edge belong to the adjoining sheet (Blatt 13, the next page), whose theses carry exactly those numbers.

The argument, restated as a sequence of postulates:
(a) Every simple act of thought deposits something permanent and substantial in the soul.
(b) This permanent thing appears as a unity. Because it is the expression of something extended in space and time, it seems to contain an inner manifold. Riemann therefore calls it 'Geistesmasse' (mind-mass).
(c) Mind-masses entering the soul appear to us as representations (Vorstellungen). The differing quality of representations is determined by the differing mental form of the mind-masses, that is, by differences in the process in which they form.
(d) Newly forming mind-masses combine to definite degrees with each other and with older ones. Their 'entry into the soul' simply consists in this combination with older masses.
(e) Hence the soul is a compact, most intimately and manifoldly interconnected mind-mass. It grows continually through newly entering masses, and its development rests on this growth.
(4) Once formed, mind-masses are imperishable and their connections indissoluble. Only the relative strength of the connections changes as new masses are added.
(5) The persistence of mind-masses and of their connections needs no material substrate, and they exert no lasting effect on the phenomenal world. So they stand in no relation to any part of matter and have no seat in space.
(6) By contrast, every formation of new mind-masses and every connection between them requires a material carrier. Hence all thinking (every act of mental life) takes place at a definite location.
(Parenthetical empirical support: retaining experiences costs no effort, only thinking does, and the expended effort is, as far as we can judge, proportional to the mental activity.)

Purpose and context: these are the postulates of a Herbartian-style mechanics of representations, meant to explain reproduction through memory and imagination (see Blatt 13). They parallel Riemann's natural-philosophical picture on the surrounding pages, where 'Stoff' streams into ponderable atoms and ceases to act on the phenomenal world. A version of this text is printed among the 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts' (Zur Psychologie und Metaphysik) in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke, edited by Weber and Dedekind in 1876.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible, since there is no mathematics on the page.
Philosophically, thesis (5) (persistence without a material substrate) and thesis (6) (formation requires a material carrier at a definite place) are posited, not derived.
The inference 'no lasting effect on the phenomenal world, therefore no seat in space' is an assumption-laden step rather than a proof.

results.what: Theory of 'Geistesmassen': imperishable mental substances formed in each act of thought; their varying connection strengths explain association, memory and the growth of the soul.
results.modern_name: Associationist / Herbartian psychology of representations (Vorstellungsmechanik); a precursor of memory-trace and connection-strength (associative network) ideas.
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart (Psychologie als Wissenschaft, 1824-25); associationism generally (Hume, Hartley). Riemann's specific 'Geistesmasse' version is his own.

results.what: Mind-matter thesis: forming and connecting mental contents requires a material carrier with a definite location, while stored contents have no spatial seat; mental effort is proportional to mental activity.
results.modern_name: Dualist account of mind-brain interaction and localisation of mental acts.
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's own formulation within 19th-century psychophysics debates (Fechner, Herbart, Lotze).

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely philosophical and contains no mathematics. Its content, Riemann's 'Geistesmasse' psychology, is already published in the philosophical fragments of his Gesammelte Werke (1876) and is well known to Riemann scholars as his Herbartian-inspired metaphysics.
transcription_corrections: 'Die Seele ist also eine compacte[?], aufs Engste': 'compacte' is supported by the parallel text on Blatt 13 ('eine compacte, aufs Innigste und Mannigfachste'). The following word in the image is hard to read and may be 'Engste' or 'Innigste'; it should be checked against the printed Werke text.

The right-edge numerals 1), 2), 3), 4), 7), 8), 10), 11) are cropped margins of the facing sheet (Blatt 13), not part of this page's text. The fragment 'un[?]' at the top right is likely the start of 'nehme ich an' / 'Zur Erklärung...' on that sheet.
'(Jeder Act unseres Seelenlebens)': the image may read 'Art', but 'Act' fits the context and the parallel wording on Blatt 13 ('in jedem Act unseres Seelenlebens').
